analysis.one_liner: Expands Medicare to cover every American, financed by removing the payroll tax cap.
analysis.headline: The bill to put every American on Medicare was referred to two House subcommittees in April 1991 with 8 cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have opened Medicare — the government health program now limited to seniors and some disabled people — to every U.S. citizen and lawful resident starting January 1, 1993, with no age restriction and no monthly premiums. It would have added pregnancy, prenatal, well-child, and routine checkup coverage, and made Medicare the first payer for everyone's care instead of a backup to private insurance. To pay for it, the bill would have removed the ceiling on wages subject to the Medicare payroll tax and let federal health officials raise the tax rate each year, while sweeping Social Security surpluses into the Medicare trust fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Every American who lacked insurance or had thin private coverage would gain full Medicare hospital and doctor benefits, including prenatal and preventive care that standard Medicare historically excluded. Lower- and middle-income workers would benefit most, since they would stop paying private premiums and their payroll tax rate would not rise above what higher earners pay; the biggest new tax burden falls on wages above the old cap, which belong to the highest earners and their employers. People with preexisting conditions who private insurers could decline or price out would be covered automatically.

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. citizen and lawful permanent resident would become entitled to full Medicare hospital (Part A) and doctor (Part B) benefits beginning January 1, 1993, with no age or disability requirement.

The Part B monthly premium would be repealed and replaced with a direct government contribution covering the full actuarial value of benefits, so beneficiaries would no longer pay premiums out of pocket.
Medicare's covered preventive services would expand to include pregnancy-related care, prenatal, postnatal, and well-child care, and routine physical checkups.

Medicare would become the primary payer for all health care, by striking the section of law that bars Medicare from paying when other insurance exists — ending the patchwork of coordination-of-benefits rules between Medicare and private plans.

Financing would come from removing the cap on wages subject to the Medicare hospital insurance tax after 1992, so high earners pay the tax on all their wages rather than only up to the annual ceiling, plus annual rate adjustments set by the Secretary of Health and Human Services.

analysis.who_pays: Workers, employers, and the self-employed would pay higher Medicare payroll taxes: after 1992 the tax would apply to unlimited wages, and the Health and Human Services Secretary would be required to raise the rate each year by enough to cover the program's added costs plus a reserve of up to 10 percent. The bill would also transfer unused surpluses from the Social Security retirement trust fund into the Medicare hospital fund. Private insurers would lose most of the under-65 insurance market.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers and employers via payroll taxes

drawbacks.text: The financing has no statutory ceiling: after 1992 the Secretary of Health and Human Services must set the Medicare payroll tax rate each December at whatever level covers estimated program costs plus a reserve of up to 10 percent, so the tax rate could rise year after year without a vote of Congress setting a limit.

Removing the wage cap means the Medicare tax would apply to every dollar of wages, a substantial tax increase aimed at the highest earners — and since employer and employee rates must stay equal, employers would face the same uncapped increase.

The bill sweeps whatever Social Security retirement (OASI) surplus the Secretary deems unneeded into the Medicare hospital insurance trust fund, drawing down the retirement system's reserves to cover health costs.

The bill repeals the premium and secondary-payer provisions wholesale with an effective date of January 1, 1993, replacing the existing mixed public-private system with Medicare as the payer for everyone on a fixed timeline, with no transition mechanism set out in the text for the displaced private coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — comprehensive health coverage for every resident, with no premiums and guaranteed preventive care — is large and would fall hardest in favor of people the existing system left out. The cost is real but borne unevenly: an uncapped, annually adjustable payroll tax on all wages, weighted toward high earners and their employers, plus a draw on the Social Security surplus. The honest weakness of the design is the open-ended financing formula — Congress would have delegated the annual tax rate to the Health and Human Services Secretary rather than setting it in law — and the abrupt January 1, 1993 cutoff with no transition plan for the private coverage it displaces.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the health subcommittees of two House committees in April 1991 and sat there — no hearing, no markup, no vote — until the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Sam Gibbons introduced the Medicare Universal Coverage Expansion Act on April 16, 1991, and it was referred jointly to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees the same day.

On April 22 the bill was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health, and on April 26 to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment — the last entries in its action history.
Six additional House Democrats signed on as additional sponsors in October 1991, bringing total support to the original sponsor plus 8 cosponsors — all Democrats, none Republican.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded at any point in the 102nd Congress; the bill died in subcommittee when the Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and employers kept the existing employment-based insurance system, and the uninsured and underinsured of 1991-1993 gained nothing. The sponsors' single-payer-style approach returned nothing until later Congresses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers kept the status quo

for.name: Sam Gibbons
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-FL), bill sponsor, senior member of House Ways and Means
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 16, 1991 to extend Medicare to the entire population.

for.name: 8 of 267 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

for.name: Fortney 'Pete' Stark and five other House Democrats
for.role: Additional sponsors (Stark of California, Bustamante, Peterson of Florida, Lewis of Georgia, Norton, Scheuer)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as additional sponsors recorded in the October 25, 1991 printing of the bill.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee and then to its Health Subcommittee on April 22, 1991; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee and then to its Health and Environment Subcommittee on April 26, 1991; no further action was ever taken.

against.name: George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: His administration opposed government-run national health insurance and backed market-based alternatives during this period.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat and no Republican supported it, but the decisive inaction came from the Democratic chairmen of the two committees where the bill sat.

industries.note: Universal Medicare with no premiums would replace the private insurance market for virtually everyone under 65, and making Medicare the primary payer strips insurers of their role coordinating benefits. The bill's death left the employer-based private insurance system intact.

Employers would stop paying private health premiums for workers but would owe an uncapped Medicare payroll tax on every dollar of wages at a rate set annually to cover the whole program. Their interest in preserving the employer-based system ran against the bill's universal coverage.

Providers would gain a guaranteed payer for every patient and an end to uncompensated care for the uninsured, but Medicare pays lower administered rates than private insurers, so revenue per patient would likely fall as Medicare became the primary payer for everyone.
